title: Building a Payment Accuracy Review Process in Healthcare
summary: Learn how to build a payment accuracy review process, validate variances, and prevent underpayments with a joint Revenue Cycle and Managed Care approach.
body_markdown:
*By Vanessa C*


**Summary:** A payment accuracy review process in hospitals involves examining remittance details to understand payment discrepancies, distinguishing between genuine underpayments and contractual adjustments, and addressing individual claim variances. It requires identifying patterns, validating root causes, and collaborating between Revenue Cycle and Managed Care teams to ensure correct reimbursement and prevent future variances, ultimately enhancing financial health and operational efficiency.


An 835 transaction lands in the patient accounting system with a paid amount $4,200 below the expected net revenue model. The collector's first reaction is to draft a dispute letter, while patient financial services is already staring at a growing queue of partial payments. An objective payment accuracy review process for hospitals settles whether that gap is an unpaid balance or a contractual write-off before staff spend hours chasing money that is not there.


Payer friction is getting worse across commercial and managed care lines. Vendor data published by[FierceHealthcare in 2025 showed that payer audits and denial amounts rose again](https://www.fiercehealthcare.com/finance/payer-audits-denial-amounts-rise-again-2025-vendor-data-show) points to a rise in denied and reduced payments, and hospital margins feel the squeeze. When every dollar matters, revenue cycle teams cannot mix up adjudication rules with payment errors.


## Start With the Remittance Detail


Start with the electronic remittance advice (ERA) 835 or the paper Explanation of Benefits, not just the balance field. Read the Claim Adjustment Reason Codes (CARC) and Remittance Advice Remark Codes (RARC) line by line against the primary contract schedule.


Check whether the reduction comes from group code PR (patient responsibility), CO (contractual obligation), or OA (other adjustment). A payer using CARC 97 for bundled procedures may still be paying correctly under an outpatient surgical grouper agreement, so an appeal would go nowhere.


## A Payment Variance Is Not Automatically an Underpayment


A gap between expected gross revenue and actual receipt often points to a modeling problem inside your own contract management system, not a payer shortfall. If an updated payer fee schedule or a revised carve-out tier never got loaded into your billing system, the expected payment calculation will fire a false alert.


According to an analysis published by[ICD10monitor, underpayment losses within commercial payer contracts can directly cut into net patient revenue](https://icd10monitor.medlearn.com/tracking-underpayments/) , the damage grows when real errors slip past review. But chasing legitimate contractual reductions burns administrative time you never get back. The[CAQH Index found that administrative automation represents a $20 billion cost-savings opportunity](https://www.ajmc.com/view/caqh-index-finds-20-billion-in-cost-savings-opportunities) across the healthcare industry keeps rising, which is why manual teams should not spend their day auditing clean adjudications.

## Treat the Claim First, Then Watch for the Pattern


When a real underpayment shows up on an active account, handle that individual claim right away through your usual dispute submission or secondary billing path. After the account is closed out, record the line-item variance in a shared tracking sheet so you can see whether it keeps happening.


One claim with the wrong DRG base rate points to an operational error. Fifty straight outpatient surgery claims from the same managed care plan paying below the agreed per-diem rate point somewhere else, usually to a system setup problem on the payer's adjudication platform.


## Quantify the Trend Before You Escalate It


You need aggregate data before you notify leadership or go to payer provider relations. Group the affected claims by National Provider Identifier (NPI), health plan ID, and procedure code so the total shortfall is visible.


A single underpayment of $400 rarely calls for formal dispute arbitration. A steady $400 shortfall across 350 inpatient surgical accounts does point to a $140,000 variance. That kind of financial weight gives joint escalation teams the pressure they need to ask the health plan for an automated mass reprocessing batch.


## Validate the Root Cause Before Blaming the Payer


Check your internal charge description master (CDM) and clearinghouse rules before accusing a health plan of non-compliance. Confirm that your billing team attached the needed modifiers, such as modifier 59 or 25, that support separate reimbursement under your contract language. If your patient access department failed to capture updated coordination of benefits information, the payer may have paid correctly as secondary rather than primary. Taking an internal billing failure outside the organization strains payer relationships and slows cash realization.


## Use a Joint Revenue Cycle and Managed Care Approach


When payment differences keep coming back and the usual dispute path goes nowhere, put patient financial services and the managed care contracting group on the same case. Revenue cycle managers bring the operational proof, including claim numbers, service dates, and 835 remittance logs. Managed care negotiators bring the contract reading and keep direct escalation channels open with plan executives.


That combined approach stops the payer from sending everything back to ordinary phone queues. It turns a pile of manual follow-up into settlement talks that have to be answered.


## Create Visibility Only If It Helps


Do not build extra tracking sheets that only record unpaid money and never assign anyone to act on it. An underpayment tracking queue should give live reporting tied to specific fields: payer name, days past adjudication, and variance size. If an operational queue turns into an unmonitored storehouse for small write-offs, attention drifts away from accounts with real recovery potential. Set up your electronic health record work queues so they flag accounts only when they meet set financial thresholds and documented contract discrepancy profiles.


## Someone Still Has to Own the Work


A dashboard will not bring cash back without clear operational ownership assigned to named teams. Revenue cycle leaders need to decide whether the patient accounting team, a dedicated variance unit, or an outside support team handles payment discrepancy follow-up. Service-level agreements keep accounts from sitting between initial billing, coding review, and payer escalation. Every variance queue needs named specialists who submit reconsideration packages and audit payer responses within 30 days after posting.


## Send the Feedback Back to the Department That Can Prevent It


Payment accuracy reviews fall short if they act only as a collections unit instead of an intelligence hub. When audit reviews show that unbundled charges or missing prior authorization numbers are driving payment cuts, send the findings straight to clinical documentation improvement (CDI) or central scheduling. A report published by[Becker's Payer Issues showed that overall claims denial rates were up while prior authorization denials fell in 2024](https://www.beckerspayer.com/payer/claims-denial-rates-up-prior-auth-denials-down-in-2024-report/) . This trend shows that clinical validation processes are getting better, yet general claims friction keeps climbing. Tightening registration and billing loops cuts off preventable variance patterns before claims clear your clearinghouse.


## Recovery Is Not the End of the Review


Getting an adjustment check from a health plan clears the balance for that encounter, but the financial leak stays open until contract terms are reinforced. If a payer keeps ignoring contracted escalator clauses on complex implants, every later case will need manual staff intervention.


According to reporting by[Healthcare Finance News, hospital net revenue leakage increased 25% due to denied claims](https://www.healthcarefinancenews.com/news/hospitals-net-revenue-leakage-increases-25-due-denied-claims) , illustrating the growing operational cost of repetitive appeals. Record every settled discrepancy as precedent so the payer has to update its automated claims adjudication logic.


This guidance applies directly to standard fee-for-service commercial contracts and Medicare Advantage arrangements. It does not apply to value-based risk pools, bundled episodic capitation models, or shared-savings programs, where payment accuracy is determined by population health quality metrics and risk-adjustment reconciliations rather than claim-by-claim fee schedule auditing.


## Corrective Action Has to Be Validated


Never treat a payer's confirmation of a configuration fix as proof that future claims will process correctly. Put active test monitoring rules on the next three adjudication batches from that health plan for the affected service lines.


Compare new 835 remittances with the revised payment schedule so reimbursement lines up with contracted rates. A corrective action process counts as successful only when production remittances post at full contracted value and no human intervention is needed.


## Track Recovery and Prevention Together


Judge payment accuracy teams on two separate operating measures, net cash collected through dispute resolution and the drop in newly created variance accounts month over month.


If you rely only on recovery figures, teams get rewarded for treating symptoms while the root issue stays in place. Tracking the average time from initial variance posting to final payer reconciliation keeps accounts from aging past statutory timely filing deadlines.


## Payment Accuracy Is More Than Recovery


Auditing payment accuracy requires extensive AR legwork, including checking payer clearinghouses, parsing denial codes, and dialing payer phone trees. To alleviate the repetitive manual labor tied to claims follow-up, health systems can deploy[LunaBill](https://lunabill.com/) to work the AR queue directly.


LunaBill uses a coordinated team of 13 specialized AI agents that navigate payer portals, place automated calls to payer representatives through complex IVR queues, extract denial notes, and submit standard appeals through your existing systems. By letting automation address the mechanical tasks of claim status verification, hospital teams can focus their operational capacity on complex managed care contract disputes.


## Conclusion


Audit the next twenty commercial payments that landed below expected net revenue inside your patient accounting system. Group them by payer, identify the applied CARC adjustment codes, and determine whether the variance stemmed from an unupdated internal fee schedule or a payer-side adjudication error.


Establishing an effective payment accuracy review process requires disciplined coordination between patient financial services and managed care contracting. Equip your team with accurate contract models, maintain focused escalation queues, and confirm that every recovered dollar leads to a permanent fix in billing logic.
